question_text:
In the text, the calculated magnetic moment of a unit cell of magnetite $\left(32 \mu_{B}\right)$ was found to be close to the measured value of $32.8 \mu_{B}$. Make a similar calculation for nickel ferrite, which has a measured value of $18.4 \mu_{B}$.

Refer to Table:
\begin{tabular}{|l|l|}
\hline \multicolumn{2}{|c|}{Magnetic Moment of Various Transition Metal Ions} \\
\hline Ion & Moment ( $\left.\mu_B\right)^{\text {a }}$ \\
\hline $\mathrm{Mn}^{2+}$ & 5 \\
\hline $\mathrm{Fe}^{2+}$ & 4 \\
\hline $\mathrm{Fe}^{3+}$ & 5 \\
\hline $\mathrm{Co}^{2+}$ & 3 \\
\hline $\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}$ & 2 \\
\hline $\mathrm{Cu}^{2+}$ & 1 \\
\hline
\end{tabular}The unit of the answer is \mu_{B}.
response:
## Reasoning

**Nickel ferrite** has the formula **NiFe₂O₄** and, like magnetite, adopts an **inverse spinel** structure. A unit cell contains 8 formula units, giving 8 Ni²⁺ ions and 16 Fe³⁺ ions.

In the inverse spinel arrangement:
- **Tetrahedral (A) sites:** 8 Fe³⁺ ions, each with moment 5 μ_B → aligned in one direction
- **Octahedral (B) sites:** 8 Ni²⁺ ions (2 μ_B each) + 8 Fe³⁺ ions (5 μ_B each) → aligned in the opposite direction

The two sublattices are antiparallel (Néel coupling), so the net moment is:

$$M_{\text{net}} = M_B - M_A = (8\times 2 + 8\times 5) - (8\times 5) = (16 + 40) - 40 = 16\;\mu_B$$

This is close to the measured value of 18.4 μ_B, just as the calculated 32 μ_B for magnetite was close to its measured 32.8 μ_B.

$$\boxed{16}$$
